preamble: The palatal lateral [ʎ] can lose its laterality and become the voiced postalveolar fricative [ʒ]. Spanish shows the change twice. In the medieval period, [ʎ] from Vulgar Latin -LJ-, -C'L-, -G'L- fricativized to Old Spanish /ʒ/ (later /ʃ/, then modern /x/), while Portuguese kept the lateral (filho, olho). In the Andean highlands of northern Ecuador, /ʎ/ (ll) is pronounced [ʒ] and stays distinct from /ʝ/ (y), so the change happened there without yeísmo. Highland Ecuadorian Kichwa has /ʒ/ for the palatal lateral of other Quechua (suffix -lla /ʒa/), matching the local Spanish pronunciation of ll.

examples.note: The sound later devoiced to /ʃ/ and backed to modern /x/.
In the Sierra of northern Ecuador, /ʎ/ is realized as [ʒ] (rehilamiento) and contrasts with /ʝ/ in yo; Argüello argues this is a realization of /ʎ/ and does not come from yeísmo.
Kichwa ⟨ll⟩ is /ʒ/; Chimborazo has punllallapimi /punʒaʒapimi/, while Cañar–Loja and Tena keep [ʎ] in the suffix (/punʒaʎapimi/).

sources: Wikipedia (2026). History of the Spanish language. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Spanish_language
